prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map supports a coarse layered layout: the camera wearer is very close to a person occupying the lower/central foreground (roughly 0.3–0.8 m), while the tabletop and objects are farther ahead (about 0.7–1.5 m), with the wall/background beyond them (roughly 1.5–3 m). It makes the person’s raised arms appear nearer than the table and separates nearby vessels and cups from the darker recesses, relationships that are harder to judge from the distorted RGB strip alone. Across the five frames, the person remains close while an arm repeatedly extends forward toward the table and upward/right in the image; the camera viewpoint also turns, changing which table objects and background areas are visible. Exact metric distances, object boundaries, and ordering near the person-table contact regions are unreliable because monocular depth has no known scale and shows broad smoothing, bright saturation, and edge bleeding.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map consistently isolates one nearby person across the five frames, including much of the torso and raised arms, showing that this person is directly in front of the camera wearer and roughly within 0.3–1 m; no second person is clearly separated. The mask clarifies the person’s silhouette and which foreground regions occlude the table, especially where an arm rises toward the upper part of each frame, but it provides little direct distance information and does not establish gaze or facing direction reliably. Over time, the person remains central and close while the visible arm configuration shifts from left/upper-left toward upper-right as the viewpoint or body orientation changes; parts of the body stay cut off by the bottom edge. The map is unreliable for objects and fine anatomy: cups, containers, cloths, and most table items are unlabeled, several body regions are fragmented or merged with nearby surfaces, and the final frame contains an overlapping duplicate-looking person mask.
descriptions.pose: The pose map is entirely black in all five frames, so it supplies no detected body or hand joints, facing direction, gaze direction, reach geometry, or motion trajectory beyond what can be seen in the RGB. From the RGB context alone, one person is very close and partly out of view below the frame, with arms extending toward the tabletop and nearby cups or containers that appear within that person’s reach and likely within about 0.5–1 m of the camera wearer. The person remains in front of the wearer across the sequence, but the changing arm positions and camera rotation cannot be quantified by this map, and no reliable conclusion about whether the person looks toward the wearer can be made. The absence of skeletons is likely a detection failure caused by severe viewpoint rotation, close cropping, occlusion, and unusual egocentric body geometry, so this map should not be treated as evidence that no person or hands are present.
